strengths: The paper addresses an important NLP problem: learning from feedback expressed naturally during multi-turn conversations. The publicly linked 20,281-pair dataset and explicit textual preference summaries constitute a concrete, interpretable resource contribution.

Experiments cover three model families, three public benchmarks, and a 540-example custom evaluation. Several improvements over the starting instruction-tuned models are substantial: Phi-3’s AlpacaEval length-controlled win rate increases from 24.3% to 34.9%, and its Arena-Hard win rate from 15.4% to 32.4%.

Regenerating UltraFeedback responses with comparable generators improves the baseline comparison. Reporting length-controlled scores, evaluations with and without checklists, and separation of training and test users/conversations are useful methodological choices.

Human validation covers feedback detection in 50 conversations and checklist-based evaluation in 200 conversations. The appendices provide rubrics, prompts, model identifiers, and key training hyperparameters, supporting substantial portions of reproduction.
weaknesses: The decisive concern is incomplete validation of better alignment with actual users. GPT-4o extracts preferences, generates preferred responses, filters on-policy pairs, and judges the custom evaluation. Consequently, improved checklist scores can reflect agreement with its inferred preferences. Appendix C reports 57.14% agreement and κ = 0.372 with human checklist-based judgments, but does not establish checklist faithfulness to original feedback or demonstrate improved human agreement relative to evaluation without checklists. Independent assessment of the trained models against original user feedback would strengthen the central claim.

The experiments do not isolate the contribution of feedback. WildFeedback and UltraFeedback differ in prompt distribution, conversational context, response construction, and filtering. A control using the same WildChat prompts and generation budget without extracted feedback would distinguish feedback benefits from conversational data selection and teacher distillation. An SFT-only baseline would also clarify the additional value of the preference pairs.

Claims of significant and consistent superiority exceed the reported evidence. No confidence intervals or variation across training seeds are supplied, although several differences from UltraFeedback are small. There are also explicit exceptions: Qwen2 trained on WF GPT-4 scores below UF GPT-4 on AlpacaEval LC (39.4 versus 40.6) and MT-Bench (7.60 versus 7.66).

The custom evaluation selects central preferences within 70 clusters and deliberately favors tasks similar to training tasks. This supports an evaluation within that selected distribution, but does not establish coverage of the majority of users or diverse, evolving preferences. The feedback detector’s 48.4% DSAT recall further limits coverage. Broad claims about resolving subjectivity and synthetic-data bias should be narrowed.

Important construction details remain underspecified, including the embedding model and clustering configuration, precise user-grouping and split procedures, generation decoding settings, and hyperparameter-selection protocol. Providing executable configurations and exact split identifiers would make the custom benchmark substantially easier to reproduce. Together with the unresolved validation and attribution concerns, these gaps leave the case for Findings borderline.
